title: Given two sorted arrays, find the median of the combined sorted order. Explain how the K-way Merge pattern locates the middle without fully merging, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Median of Two Sorted Arrays (K-way Merge View of the Middle Element)

s1_definition.profdef: Median of Two Sorted Arrays, viewed through the K-way Merge pattern, advances a two-way merge only up to the middle position rather than merging everything. We keep the two array heads as candidates, repeatedly take the smaller, and stop once we have passed the middle index or indices. For a combined length that is odd the single middle value is the median; for even we average the two middle values. This merge-to-the-middle runs in linear time in the total length.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has two sorted lists of account balances and wants the middle balance of the combined set. A clerk walks both lists together, always taking the smaller next balance, counting steps, and stops at the middle. There is no need to write out the whole combined list.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two-way merge, but stop at the middle position to read off the median.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Median of Two Sorted Arrays, viewed through the K-way Merge pattern, advances a two-way merge only up to the middle position rather than merging everything. We keep the two array heads as candidates, repeatedly take the smaller, and stop once we have passed the middle index or indices. For a combined length that is odd the single middle value is the median; for even we average the two middle values. This merge-to-the-middle runs in linear time in the total length.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has two sorted lists of account balances and wants the middle balance of the combined set. A clerk walks both lists together, always taking the smaller next balance, counting steps, and stops at the middle. There is no need to write out the whole combined list.

**One line to remember:** Two-way merge, but stop at the middle position to read off the median.

sections.s2_technical:
We treat the two arrays as two sorted lists in a K-way merge with K equal to two. We keep an index into each array and compare the current heads, advancing whichever is smaller. We count how many elements we have consumed and keep the last one or two values needed for the median.

For combined length `n`, if `n` is odd the median is the value at consumed position `n/2` (zero-based), and if `n` is even it is the average of the values at positions `n/2 - 1` and `n/2`. We therefore only need to merge up to `n/2` steps and remember the previous value. A concrete comparison is `if (j >= b.length || (i < a.length && a[i] <= b[j])) take a[i++]; else take b[j++];`. Senior nuance: for money we average with BigDecimal to avoid precision loss, and although a full binary-search solution reaches log time, the merge-to-the-middle view is the clear K-way Merge framing and is linear, which is perfectly acceptable to explain in an interview as the pattern-based answer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps two sorted lists of customer balances from two regions and the analytics team needs the median balance of the two regions combined to report a typical customer. Concatenating and sorting is wasteful because each list is already sorted. This is exactly how the merge-to-the-middle view works: it walks both lists together only as far as the middle.

The code defines a `MedianBalanceService` exposing `median(a, b)` returning a BigDecimal median. A `Demo` builds two sorted balance arrays and logs the combined median.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is region A with 10000, 25000, 40000 and region B with 15000, 30000, 50000, 60000. The combined length is seven, so the median is the value at consumed position three in zero-based terms, which means we merge four steps.

Step 1 — Indices start at zero. We compare 10000 and 15000, take 10000 from A, consumed one, current is 10000.

Step 2 — Compare 25000 and 15000, take 15000 from B, consumed two, current is 15000.

Step 3 — Compare 25000 and 30000, take 25000 from A, consumed three, current is 25000.

Step 4 — Compare 40000 and 30000, take 30000 from B, consumed four, current is 30000. We have now consumed four elements, passing the middle index three, so we stop.

Step 5 — The combined length seven is odd, so the median is the current value at the middle, 30000. The result is shown below.

```

INFO: Median balance = Rs.30000
Oct 27, 2026 8:51:30 PM com.bank.median.MedianBalanceApplication main

```

    │ take 15000 (B)  consumed 2

sections.s6_takeaway:
Median of Two Sorted Arrays, framed through the K-way Merge pattern, is a two-way merge that I stop at the middle instead of running to completion. I keep an index into each array, repeatedly take the smaller of the two current heads, and count how many elements I have consumed. Because both arrays are already sorted, walking them together produces the combined order element by element, and I only need to reach the middle position.

For the combined length I decide the median rule up front. If the total is odd, the median is the single value sitting at the middle consumed position. If the total is even, it is the average of the two middle values, so I remember both the previous and the current value as I merge. For balances I average using BigDecimal so I never lose a paisa to floating-point error. This merge-to-the-middle view is linear in the total length, which is a clean and correct pattern answer even though a binary-search version can reach logarithmic time.

At the National Bank of India I used this to report a typical customer balance across two regions whose balance lists were each already sorted. I merged the two lists only as far as the middle and read off the median, averaging with BigDecimal when the combined count was even. Explaining that this is a K-way Merge with K equal to two, that I stop at the middle rather than merging everything, and that I handle odd and even lengths separately is what shows an interviewer I can map a classic median question onto the merge pattern.
